opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think chopsticks are a really nice testbed, partly for practical reasons and partly for deeper ones.

On the practical side, chopsticks are incredibly simple hardware. It's just two sticks. You don't need an expensive multi-fingered hand with dozens of motors and tactile sensors that break all the time. You can build a chopsticks robot cheaply, it's robust, and you can run a lot of experiments on it. For a researcher that matters a lot, because the bottleneck in robot learning is often just how much you can actually run on real hardware.

But the more interesting part is that even though the hardware is simple, the task is not. Using chopsticks well requires fine, precise control. You're picking up small things, slippery things, sometimes tiny objects, and the margin for error is very small. If your position is off by a few millimeters, or the timing of closing is slightly wrong, the object slips or flies away. So it exposes the weaknesses of a manipulation algorithm very clearly. You can't hide behind a big gripper that just grabs anything.

It's also a tool-use problem. Humans aren't born knowing how to use chopsticks. We learn it, and how well we do varies a lot. That makes it a nice analogy for the kind of skill learning we want robots to have: you take a simple tool and, through practice and good control, get really dexterous behavior out of it. I find that kind of setting appealing because it separates the question "how good is your hardware" from "how good is your intelligence and control."

And honestly, there's a cultural, intuitive piece too. Everybody understands immediately what it means to be good at chopsticks. When you show a video of a robot picking up a peanut or a small ball with chopsticks, people instantly get how hard that is. So it's a good way to communicate what fine manipulation really means.

r001.rationale: The response explains why chopstick manipulation is difficult and useful for evaluating control, but it does not say that succeeding at it suggests the algorithm can handle easier manipulation tasks.

fable-5.1.text:
Chopsticks are deceptively hard. People think of them as a simple tool, but when you actually look at what the hand is doing, it's one of the most demanding manipulation tasks in everyday life. You have two rigid sticks, you're controlling them with only one hand, one stick is basically fixed and the other pivots, and you have to coordinate finger forces precisely enough to grip something as small as a single grain of rice or as slippery as a piece of tofu without crushing it.

So for me it's a very honest benchmark. A lot of robotic grasping results look good because the gripper is forgiving. A parallel-jaw gripper will tolerate a few millimeters of error and still succeed. Chopsticks don't give you that. If your pose estimate is off by a couple millimeters, or your force control is slightly too aggressive, the object slips or breaks. The task exposes every weakness in perception, in control, and in the way the two are coupled. You cannot hide behind the hardware.

The other reason is that it's a tool-use problem, not just a grasping problem. The robot isn't contacting the object directly. It's contacting a tool, and the tool contacts the object. That extra layer means the robot has to reason about something it can't directly sense, which is exactly the situation we care about if we want robots to pick up a human tool and use it, rather than always designing a special end-effector for each job. If an algorithm works on chopsticks, I have much more confidence it will generalize to screwdrivers, tweezers, spoons, whatever.

And honestly, there's a cultural piece too. Chopsticks are something most people in China learn as children, and it feels a bit like a rite of passage. There's something satisfying about asking whether a robot can pass the same test a five-year-old can.

r001.rationale: The response says chopsticks are a demanding benchmark and that success with them gives confidence the algorithm will generalize to other tools and tasks.

astra-6.text:
I like chopsticks because they’re simple tools, but using them well is surprisingly difficult. You have to coordinate the two tips, make precise contact with an object, and apply enough force to hold it without crushing it or letting it slip. Small errors really matter.

They’re also versatile. With the same pair of chopsticks, you can pick up objects with very different shapes, sizes, and textures. So they give us a useful test: can the algorithm adapt to those differences, or has it just learned one very specific grasp? It’s an everyday task that exposes a lot of the challenges in robotic manipulation.

r001.rationale: The response describes chopstick use as a challenging, versatile test of adaptation, but does not say that success may predict easier success on other manipulation tasks.

sol-6.1.text: I like chopsticks because they turn a simple everyday task into a really rich manipulation problem. You have to control two thin tools precisely, make contact in the right places, and apply enough force to hold an object without crushing it or letting it slip. And the challenge changes depending on what you’re picking up—something small, soft, or slippery. So it’s a compact way to test whether an algorithm can handle precise motion and delicate contact together.
